author: host-coordinator
text:
**I recommend this separation. It is achievable and would give HAI a clearer, more useful distinction between roles and skills.** However, it requires more than removing HAI references from the text.

I reviewed all **12 distinct skills**, including source and installed copies. The complete findings are in the [skill portability review](C:/Users/hmhri/Desktop/repos/HAI/.hai_env/activities/00000000_000000_active/results/skill-portability-review.md).

The current situation:

- `crete-design-package` already follows your proposed approach.
- Specification management has an independent core, mixed with HAI configuration and integration.
- Most other skills require HAI Activities, conventions, saved settings or runtime helpers.
- Role authoring, workflow authoring, framework advice and release management contain substantial HAI-specific knowledge. They need deliberate separation of reusable methods from HAI instructions.

The previous implementation enabled skills to run **without selecting a role**. It did not make them independent of HAI. Your observation identifies a real remaining architectural issue.

I recommend these boundaries:

| Component | What belongs there |
|---|---|
| **Skill** | Reusable method, input/output expectations, templates, scripts and genuine prerequisites. |
| **Role** | Responsibilities, authority, skill selection and HAI-specific usage: conventions, configuration, locations and handoffs. |
| **Workflow** | Order of work, responsible roles, artifact transfers, conditions, loops and human approvals. |
| **HAI framework** | Activity lifecycle, recording, persistence, configuration validation and workflow execution. |

For example, a requirements-analysis skill should know how to clarify a request. The Business analyst role should supply HAI context and expected deliverables. The framework should save the records; the workflow should decide what happens next.

This broadly matches the distinction between task-specific skills, specialist roles, persistent project instructions and tools described in [GitHub’s customization guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/customizations/comparing-customizations). The [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification) supports portable packages with declared dependencies, although it also permits product-specific skills.

**The benefits are worthwhile:** easier external skill adoption, reuse outside HAI, fewer dependencies on HAI’s folder structure, and simpler upstream updates. The main risk is moving duplicated HAI instructions into every role. Shared operational rules should remain in the framework.

There is one limit to the copy-and-paste expectation: a portable skill can still require Python, Git, particular tools or service access. HAI must also discover its folder and support its metadata. The current parser and installation behavior have interoperability limitations, documented in the review.

I recommend agreeing on these boundaries, then demonstrating them with one simple skill, one script-bearing skill and one external skill before changing the entire library.

No skills, roles or runtime files were changed. This assessment is based on static inspection and primary-source research; end-to-end portability remains to be demonstrated.

author: host-coordinator
text:
**I would keep these roles and skills optional, but include them automatically in the standard HAI setup.** Users should not have to install them individually for a normal installation.

The key distinction is between a capability HAI must provide and a specialist that helps people use it:

| Capability | Where it belongs |
|---|---|
| Define the role and workflow formats | Core `.hai/` |
| Validate, install and register packages | Core `.hai/` |
| Execute workflows and maintain their state | Core `.hai/` |
| Help a person design a good role or workflow | Authoring roles and skills |

The core already provides much of the first group. The prefixed roles and skills provide the second: specialist instructions for creating and reviewing definitions.

**They are useful in most workspaces, but they are not necessary in every workspace.** An installation may only execute established workflows and use existing roles. It might never author either. HAI should also remain capable of installing its first role without needing a role-definition manager already installed.

Moving all authoring instructions into the core would make them mandatory framework material, increase the core’s maintenance scope, and make independent updates or replacements harder. Their HAI-specific nature alone does not make them core functionality.

Your concern about repeated installation is valid, though. I recommend solving it through installation defaults:

- **Standard setup:** automatically install and register both administration roles and their skills.
- **Minimal setup:** install the core alone; add authoring packages when needed.
- Keep one maintained source for each package and let installation create its environment copy.

This also makes ownership clearer: HAI maintains and distributes these packages, while a workspace can choose whether to use them or maintain a customized installed copy.

I would move an instruction into `.hai/` when **HAI requires it to function correctly regardless of which optional roles are installed**. I would retain instructions for producing good definitions in the authoring skills.

So my recommendation is: **make these standard included capabilities, rather than mandatory core components.** That gives new users a complete setup without making every installation carry the same specialists.

- Inspect the collection before changing it.
- Follow a supplied record format.
- Preserve identities, history and unrelated information.
- Keep an index consistent with its records.
- Detect concurrent changes and report partial failures.

It would receive the specific collection rules as input. For Backlog-manager, those rules could specify:

- Items have What, Why and Acceptance Criteria sections.

- The catalogue has specified columns and ordering.

|---|---|
| Backlog-manager | Work-item fields, backlog statuses and completion requirements. |
| Risk-manager | Probability, impact, mitigation, ownership and risk lifecycle. |
| Decision-recorder | Decision, rationale, alternatives and supersession rules. |

Someone outside HAI could provide the same format document directly and use the skill without any role.

2. **Extract structured records** produces candidate items and identifies missing information.
3. **Backlog-manager** resolves necessary decisions and authorizes the intended changes.
4. **Maintain a Markdown collection** writes and checks the records using the supplied backlog conventions.

I used Exa to screen **85 results across six research angles** and examine relevant material from **30 source pages**: official documentation, GitHub implementations, practitioner writing, LinkedIn and Hacker News discussions, management publications and scientific research.

**Your concern is supported: a role can legitimately own conventions, procedures and scripts. Moving everything into skills is not an established best practice.** I would withdraw the assumption behind my earlier six-skill split.

The strongest distinction is:

> **A role owns a job and its operating context. A skill provides an independently useful capability. Both may need instructions, conventions and code.**

Several findings matter for HAI.

**1. Portability does not require genericity.**

The Agent Skills specification allows procedures, scripts, templates and domain references. Anthropic’s published examples include company-specific internal communications and its own brand guidelines. A useful skill can therefore be specialized while remaining independently usable. HAI-independent skills remain a reasonable HAI design choice; making every skill applicable to every domain would be a much stronger restriction. [Specification](https://agentskills.io/specification), [company-specific skill example](https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/skills/brand-guidelines/SKILL.md)

**2. Specialist roles can retain their working methods.**

GitHub distinguishes specialist agent profiles from task-specific skills. In an actual implementation, the `wshobson/agents` repository offers separate skills while retaining a detailed working approach inside its backend-architect definition. This demonstrates a hybrid arrangement, although it does not prove that particular implementation performs best. [GitHub guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/customizations/comparing-customizations), [agent definition](https://github.com/wshobson/agents/blob/main/plugins/backend-development/agents/backend-architect.md)

Barry Zhang and Mahesh Murag advocate packaging procedural expertise instead of rebuilding agent infrastructure for every domain. That supports reusable skills; it does not establish that a logical job definition must surrender every job-specific procedure. [Their published talk materials](https://ai.engineer/talks/CEvIs9y1uog-agent-skills)

**3. More decomposition can make selection and execution worse.**

LangChain’s Robert Xu reports incorrect selection among roughly 20 similar skills, improving after consolidation to 12 in that particular setup. Vercel found that an available skill went unused in 56% of its evaluation cases. These results support clear boundaries and reliable loading of essential instructions—not a universal skill count. [LangChain evaluation](https://www.langchain.com/blog/evaluating-skills), [Vercel evaluation](https://vercel.com/blog/agents-md-outperforms-skills-in-our-agent-evals)

The SkillsBench preprint also reports benefits from focused, curated skills and weaker results from excessive content. It does **not** establish where HAI should put each procedure. [SkillsBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12670)

**4. The real-company analogy supports a richer role package.**

O*NET separates workers’ capabilities from job tasks and context. NIST describes work roles through responsibility, tasks, knowledge and skills. A job is consequently more than a collection of transferable abilities. [O*NET](https://www.onetcenter.org/content.html), [NIST NICE](https://www.nist.gov/itl/applied-cybersecurity/nice/nice-framework-resource-center/resources/occupations-jobs-and-work)

An illustrative company analogy is:

| Company element | HAI counterpart |
|---|---|
| Job description: accountability, decisions, limits | Role definition |
| Department operating manual and job-specific checklists | Role-owned conventions and procedures |
| Reusable professional practice or toolkit | Skill |
| Company-wide policy | Shared project/core convention |
| Process involving several employees | Workflow |

An AI skill package resembles a reusable practice guide more closely than a human ability. Treating those as identical can encourage artificial splitting.

For **Backlog-manager**, my provisional recommendation is:

| Current material | Recommended treatment |
|---|---|
| Responsibility, completion authority and acceptance obligations | Keep with the role |
| Backlog fields, IDs, statuses and lifecycle rules | Keep under one backlog owner |
| Importing into that backlog and preserving its evidence | Keep as a role procedure |
| HAI configuration and Activity linkage | Keep with the role, using core services |
| Backlog-specific auditor | May remain a role-owned script |
| A capability useful independently of backlog management | Consider a separate skill |

The important point is that **a role package can itself be shareable across HAI workspaces**. Reusing its operating manual in several installations does not automatically make every chapter an independent skill.

I would also keep item updates, catalogue consistency and revision safeguards cohesive. Separating them into independently selected capabilities creates additional handoffs and failure cases. This follows Parnas’s modularity principle of grouping related design decisions rather than merely turning processing steps into modules; applying it to HAI is my architectural inference. [Parnas](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/361598.361623)

My recommendation is therefore to make Backlog-manager a **complete job package with a concise entry point and supporting resources**, calling independent skills where useful. Extract a skill when it has:

- A clear independent outcome.
- Sufficient explicit inputs and understandable outputs.
- Useful application outside the owning role.
- A demonstrated benefit from separate ownership and discovery.

I found no controlled study establishing one optimal HAI split. Before implementation, compare a cohesive role-owned arrangement with a small extracted-capability arrangement on real import, revision, audit and completion tasks. Measure correctness, selection mistakes, recovery, effort and readability.

The [full research report and source register](C:/Users/hmhri/Desktop/repos/HAI/.hai_env/activities/00000000_000000_active/results/role-skill-boundaries-research.md) include competing approaches, named experts, community opinions, organizational research and evidence limitations.
